transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because I got written up at work last week. I'm a cashier, and I just keep getting stuck doing things at the register that don't really fit the moment. Like, I'll be standing there and I just start tapping the scanner in a pattern. Tap, tap, tap. It's one of those older handheld laser scanners, actually, not the built-in flatbed ones they have at the big grocery chains. I always preferred the flatbed ones, they remind me of the copy machines we used to use back when I was getting my bachelor's degree. The campus library had this huge Xerox machine that always smelled strongly of ozone and warm paper. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, I'll be tapping the scanner, or I'll just completely freeze with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. Just frozen there, and the customer is just standing there waiting for their change. This one guy the other day was buying three packs of peppermint gum and a daily newspaper. Who even reads the physical newspaper anymore? I mean, the ink gets all over your fingers and smudges everything you touch. But yeah, my manager saw me frozen over the drawer with the customer waiting and gave me a formal write-up, so... I guess that's why I'm here.

When you're tapping the scanner or freezing over the drawer, do you feel like you're doing it on purpose to relieve some urge or anxiety, or does it just happen to you without you being able to stop it?

Well, I'm not really sure if I'm doing it on purpose. I haven't really thought about it like an urge or anything like that. It's more like... I just realize it's happening, or I'm just stuck. Like someone just hit the pause button on me. 

You know, speaking of pause buttons, did you ever have one of those old VCRs where if you hit pause, the picture would get all fuzzy and jittery with those white tracking lines? We had this heavy silver Panasonic one right after I finished my bachelor's. I used to pause movies all the time just to read the titles of the books on the shelves in the background of a scene. I had hundreds of books myself back then. Mostly biographies and some old geology textbooks. I actually had to leave a lot of them behind in boxes when I moved into my current place because they were just too heavy to carry up the stairs. It's a third-floor walk-up, and the wooden handrail is completely loose. I've told my landlord, Gary, about it like three times, but he's always too busy fixing up his boat. He's got this old fiberglass speedboat parked right in the alley behind the dumpsters, and the tarp he keeps on it is always flapping in the wind... 

But, um, I don't know about anxiety. I just get stuck.

During these moments when you freeze over the drawer, are you fully aware of what's happening around you and can recall it afterward, or do you lose track of time and have trouble remembering what happened during that episode?

I mean, I think I know what's happening. I don't think I lose track of time, really, or... well, I'm not entirely sure. I just know I'm looking down at the open drawer. You know, staring at all the compartments with the bills and the coins. 

People still pay with exact change a lot, especially the older folks who come in early in the morning. They pull out these little leather coin purses that snap at the top. My aunt had one of those. It was red leather, and she used to keep butterscotch candies in it along with her quarters. The candies always tasted a little bit like copper, which is funny because pennies aren't even made of mostly copper anymore. They changed that back in the early eighties, I think. 1982? Because the copper was worth more than the penny itself. It's like how they used to put real silver in quarters and dimes. I actually always check the rims of the quarters when I'm working the register to see if there's a solid silver line, just in case. If you find one from before 1965, it's 90 percent silver. I found one a few years ago and put it in my pocket, but then it went through the wash and I lost it in the lint trap of the dryer. 

But, um... yeah, I'm just standing there looking at the drawer, so I guess I remember being there. I don't know if I'm fully aware of everything else, though.
When you notice yourself frozen over the cash drawer, about how long does that episode usually last—just a few seconds, or does it go on for a minute or longer before you 'come back'?

I'd say it's probably just a few seconds, maybe up to a minute? Like I said, I'll just be frozen there with my hand hovering right over the cash drawer while the customer is standing there waiting. That's exactly why I got written up last week, because my manager saw me stuck like that, not doing anything that fit the moment. 

Speaking of managers, my first manager right out of college was this guy named Phil. He wore these terrible clip-on ties. You could always tell because the knot was way too perfect, and sometimes it would sit a little crooked on his collar. He drove this old station wagon with wood paneling on the sides. I always thought those cars looked like boats on wheels. My grandfather had a real boat, a pontoon he kept down at the lake. We used to go fishing for bluegill on Sunday mornings. We’d use these little red wiggler worms that we’d dig up from the compost pile behind his garage. The compost always smelled like coffee grounds and rotten orange peels. He drank his coffee black, out of this heavy ceramic mug that had a chip on the rim. I actually chipped my front tooth once on a coffee mug... 

But, um, yeah. Just a few seconds to a minute, I think, and then I kind of snap out of it.

During these freezing episodes, do you or others notice you making any small repetitive movements—like lip-smacking, chewing motions, or fumbling with your hands or clothing—that you're not aware of doing?

I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that, anyway. Nobody's ever said anything about me smacking my lips or fumbling around. I mean, my hands are just hovering there. 

Hovering... you know, I saw this documentary once about hummingbirds and how they hover. Their wings beat something like eighty times a second. It's incredible. They have to eat constantly just to keep their energy up, mostly nectar. I tried putting up a hummingbird feeder outside my window last spring. I boiled the sugar water myself—four parts water to one part sugar, no red dye, because the dye is actually bad for them. I waited for weeks, but all I got were these huge wasps. Yellowjackets, I think. They built a nest right up under the eaves of the roof. I tried spraying it with that foam stuff that shoots twenty feet, but the wind caught it and it blew back all over my glasses. I had to scrub them with dish soap for ten minutes to get the sticky residue off. I've worn glasses since I was eight. I actually need a new prescription, the words on the register screen are starting to look a little blurry at the edges...

But, uh, no, I don't think I'm making any weird movements or chewing or anything. Just stuck.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or had thoughts or beliefs that other people have told you seem unusual or untrue?

Well, yeah, I do hear things sometimes. Most days, actually. It sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me, you know? Sometimes they'll call my name from the stockroom, or they'll tell me I rang something up wrong. But when I turn around to look, there's nobody there, and the other cashiers never hear it. 

The stockroom at work is a mess, by the way. Boxes stacked everywhere, mostly the seasonal stuff. Right now it's all the Halloween candy and those little plastic pumpkins. I always loved Halloween when I was a kid. My mom made me this incredible astronaut costume when I was ten. She used two empty two-liter soda bottles for the oxygen tanks and painted them silver. She used spray paint, the kind that smells really strong and makes you dizzy if you don't use it outside. We painted them on the driveway, and there was a silver outline of the bottles on the concrete for years. My dad tried power washing it off once, but it didn't really work. He loved that power washer. He used it on everything—the siding, the deck, even the hubcaps on his truck. It was a Ford F-150, bright red. He kept it so clean you could see your reflection in the bumper. 

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, the voices. Yeah, it's just like people talking or telling me I made a mistake on the register, but nobody's ever there when I check.
Do you notice these voices happening around the same time as when you freeze up at the register, or do they also happen at other times when you're not frozen?

Well, I don't really know if they happen at the exact same time. It's hard to tell. They definitely happen at other times, though, like when I'm just stocking shelves or wiping down the counter. 

Counters are so hard to keep clean, especially with the hand sanitizer dispenser right there. People always pump it too hard and it drips down the side of the cabinet and onto the floor. It leaves this sticky spot that catches all the dirt from people's shoes. I tried scrubbing it with this heavy-duty degreaser we have in the back, but the smell gave me a terrible headache. It smelled like cheap pine needles and chemicals. My grandmother used to use Pine-Sol on her kitchen floors. She had this old linoleum that was patterned to look like brick, but it was peeling in the corners. She used to make the best snickerdoodles in that kitchen. She'd let me roll the dough in the cinnamon sugar before she put them on the baking sheet. I still remember the way the kitchen smelled when they were baking. I tried to find her recipe after she passed away, but it was just written on the back of an old envelope and I think it got thrown out. 

But, um, yeah, I'm not really sure if the voices happen when I freeze up. They just happen kind of throughout the day, you know?

After you 'snap out of' one of these freezing episodes, do you notice feeling unusually tired, confused, sore, or having bitten your tongue or lost control of your bladder—things that might suggest your body just went through a seizure?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm usually a little tired after a long shift, but not unusually tired or anything. And I definitely haven't bitten my tongue or peed my pants or anything like that. That sounds awful. 

I did bite my tongue really bad once when I was a kid, though. I was riding my bike down this huge hill near my house—we called it Dead Man's Hill. It was so steep that if you didn't hit the brakes right at the bottom, you'd go flying right into Mr. Henderson's prize-winning rose bushes. He was so protective of those roses. He used to sit on his porch with a glass of iced tea just watching them. It was sweet tea, the real Southern kind where you boil the water with the sugar already in it so it dissolves perfectly. My wife tried to make sweet tea like that once, but she used Splenda and it just wasn't the same. It had this weird metallic aftertaste. We ended up pouring the whole pitcher down the sink. The sink in our kitchen drains really slow anyway. I think there's a clog somewhere deep in the pipes. I tried using that liquid drain cleaner, the thick gel kind that's supposed to eat through hair and grease, but it didn't really do much. I probably need to call a plumber, but they charge an arm and a leg just to show up. 

But, uh, no. I don't feel confused or sore or anything like that after I freeze up. I just kind of go back to ringing up the groceries.

Do you have any medical conditions—like thyroid problems, seizures, head injuries, or recent illnesses—or do you use alcohol or drugs, that started around the same time these freezing episodes and voices began?

No, I don't have any medical problems like that. My thyroid is fine, I think, and I definitely haven't hit my head. And I don't do drugs. I might have a beer on the weekend or something, but that's it. 

My brother is the one who's really into beer. He actually brews his own in his garage. It smells awful when he's doing it, like boiling yeast and old bread. He's got all these giant glass jugs—carboys, he calls them—lined up on his workbench. That workbench is incredible, actually. He built it himself out of reclaimed barn wood. He drove all the way out to Pennsylvania with his trailer to get the wood from this guy who was tearing down a dairy barn from the 1800s. The wood is so heavy. It's oak, I think. Or maybe chestnut? They used to use a lot of chestnut before that blight wiped them all out in the early nineteen-hundreds. It's a real shame. I read an article once that said the entire East Coast used to be covered in American chestnut trees, and the canopy was so thick that a squirrel could travel from Maine to Georgia without ever touching the ground. Can you imagine that? Just jumping from branch to branch for hundreds of miles. 

But, um, what was the question? Oh, right, illnesses and stuff. No, I haven't been sick or started drinking heavy or anything like that when all this started. I'm pretty healthy.
How long have you been experiencing these voices and freezing episodes in total—did they start a few weeks ago, or have they been going on for several months or longer?

Well, I'd say the voices and those times where I just kind of... stop, the freezing up, it's been about three months now. Three months. 

That was right around the time the leaves started changing. Autumn is my favorite time of year, honestly. The colors are just spectacular, especially up in the mountains. My wife and I used to rent this little cabin up near Asheville every October. It had this wraparound porch with a hot tub on the back deck. Sitting in that hot tub with a cup of coffee while the air was crisp and the leaves were falling... there's really nothing like it. We stopped going, though, after they raised the rental rates. It just got too expensive, you know? Everything is getting so expensive these days. I went to buy a carton of eggs the other day and I couldn't believe the price. It makes you want to start raising your own chickens. My neighbor, Gary, he has chickens in his backyard. He built this elaborate coop out of old pallets and chicken wire. He even put a little ramp in for them to walk up. Sometimes he brings us over a dozen fresh eggs. They taste so much better than the ones from the store. The yolks are this deep, rich orange color instead of pale yellow. You can really tell the difference when you make an omelet. 

But yeah, three months. That's about how long it's been going on.

Before these voices and freezing episodes started three months ago, did you notice any earlier changes—like becoming more withdrawn, having trouble concentrating, or feeling like something was 'off'—that may have begun even further back, say four to six months ago or more?

Well, yeah, I guess things were feeling off long before the freezing up started. It's actually been building for a while... about two years and four months, I'd say. That was right since my youngest left the Eastern Shore for college. 

The Eastern Shore is really beautiful, you know. We used to go out there and get those big bushel baskets of blue crabs. You lay out the newspaper on the picnic table and just go at them with those little wooden mallets. The Old Bay seasoning gets absolutely everywhere. It gets under your fingernails, and if you have a papercut you didn't know about, boy, you feel it then. My youngest loved it out there. But then he packed up his Honda Civic to head off to school. It was one of those older Civics, the ones that run forever if you just remember to change the oil. I always told him, "Check the oil every time you get gas," but kids don't listen. They just rely on the dashboard lights. The check engine light came on once when we were driving to a hardware store. I was going to buy caulk for the bathtub because the grout was getting all dark and moldy. I saw this video online about how to scrape it out and redo it. It looked so easy in the video, but the guy had this special oscillating power tool. I just had a flathead screwdriver, and let me tell you, it took me all weekend to scrape that old stuff out. My knees were killing me by Sunday night from kneeling on the tile. 

But, um... yeah. Two years and four months. That's when I started feeling like things were changing, right after he left.

doctor.question: When you notice yourself frozen over the cash drawer, about how long does that episode usually last—just a few seconds, or does it go on for a minute or longer before you 'come back'?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I came in because at the register I keep getting stuck doing things that don’t fit the moment, like tapping the scanner in a pattern or freezing with my hand over the cash drawer while the customer is waiting, and last week it got me written up.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the freezing episodes at the cash register, which is part of the disorganized/abnormal behavior symptom (S022) described in the manifestation.

patient.answer:
I'd say it's probably just a few seconds, maybe up to a minute? Like I said, I'll just be frozen there with my hand hovering right over the cash drawer while the customer is standing there waiting. That's exactly why I got written up last week, because my manager saw me stuck like that, not doing anything that fit the moment. 

Speaking of managers, my first manager right out of college was this guy named Phil. He wore these terrible clip-on ties. You could always tell because the knot was way too perfect, and sometimes it would sit a little crooked on his collar. He drove this old station wagon with wood paneling on the sides. I always thought those cars looked like boats on wheels. My grandfather had a real boat, a pontoon he kept down at the lake. We used to go fishing for bluegill on Sunday mornings. We’d use these little red wiggler worms that we’d dig up from the compost pile behind his garage. The compost always smelled like coffee grounds and rotten orange peels. He drank his coffee black, out of this heavy ceramic mug that had a chip on the rim. I actually chipped my front tooth once on a coffee mug... 

But, um, yeah. Just a few seconds to a minute, I think, and then I kind of snap out of it.

doctor.intent: Assess for automatisms (e.g., lip-smacking, chewing, fumbling movements) during the freezing episodes, which would suggest complex partial seizures rather than catatonia or a primary psychotic/developmental process
doctor.question: During these freezing episodes, do you or others notice you making any small repetitive movements—like lip-smacking, chewing motions, or fumbling with your hands or clothing—that you're not aware of doing?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about automatisms (small repetitive movements like lip-smacking, chewing, or fumbling) often associated with seizures, which is not covered by the Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior symptom profile or any other symptom in the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that, anyway. Nobody's ever said anything about me smacking my lips or fumbling around. I mean, my hands are just hovering there. 

Hovering... you know, I saw this documentary once about hummingbirds and how they hover. Their wings beat something like eighty times a second. It's incredible. They have to eat constantly just to keep their energy up, mostly nectar. I tried putting up a hummingbird feeder outside my window last spring. I boiled the sugar water myself—four parts water to one part sugar, no red dye, because the dye is actually bad for them. I waited for weeks, but all I got were these huge wasps. Yellowjackets, I think. They built a nest right up under the eaves of the roof. I tried spraying it with that foam stuff that shoots twenty feet, but the wind caught it and it blew back all over my glasses. I had to scrub them with dish soap for ten minutes to get the sticky residue off. I've worn glasses since I was eight. I actually need a new prescription, the words on the register screen are starting to look a little blurry at the edges...

But, uh, no, I don't think I'm making any weird movements or chewing or anything. Just stuck.

inference.note: Absence of automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing, fumbling) makes classic complex partial seizure with automatisms less likely but doesn't rule out atypical absence or frontal focal seizures; freezing episodes with brief duration and looking/staring remain consistent with catatonic-like stupor (F06.1/F20.9) or seizure activity (G40.909). Tangential, circumstantial speech with intense focus on minor details continues to support autism spectrum traits (F84.0) or thought disorder in schizophrenia (F20.9). No new features narrow the differential further.

doctor.intent: Screen for psychotic symptoms (hallucinations or unusual beliefs) that would support schizophrenia over the other diagnoses
doctor.question: Have you ever heard voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or had thoughts or beliefs that other people have told you seem unusual or untrue?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Most days I hear what sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me, sometimes calling my name from the stockroom or saying I rang something up wrong, but when I turn around there’s nobody there and no one else heard it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, which directly corresponds to the Hallucinations symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I do hear things sometimes. Most days, actually. It sounds like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me, you know? Sometimes they'll call my name from the stockroom, or they'll tell me I rang something up wrong. But when I turn around to look, there's nobody there, and the other cashiers never hear it. 

The stockroom at work is a mess, by the way. Boxes stacked everywhere, mostly the seasonal stuff. Right now it's all the Halloween candy and those little plastic pumpkins. I always loved Halloween when I was a kid. My mom made me this incredible astronaut costume when I was ten. She used two empty two-liter soda bottles for the oxygen tanks and painted them silver. She used spray paint, the kind that smells really strong and makes you dizzy if you don't use it outside. We painted them on the driveway, and there was a silver outline of the bottles on the concrete for years. My dad tried power washing it off once, but it didn't really work. He loved that power washer. He used it on everything—the siding, the deck, even the hubcaps on his truck. It was a Ford F-150, bright red. He kept it so clean you could see your reflection in the bumper. 

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right, the voices. Yeah, it's just like people talking or telling me I made a mistake on the register, but nobody's ever there when I check.

inference.note: Added auditory hallucinations (voices calling name, commenting on errors) without insight, which strongly supports a primary psychotic disorder (F20.9) and makes autism spectrum disorder (F84.0) unlikely, so F84.0 is dropped. Catatonic-like freezing and hallucinations keep F06.1 (catatonia due to medical condition) and G40.909 (possible absence/seizure-related freezing) still under consideration pending further neurological/organic workup.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the auditory hallucinations occur specifically during or right before the freezing episodes (suggesting an ictal phenomenon) or happen independently at other times (suggesting a primary psychotic process)
doctor.question: Do you notice these voices happening around the same time as when you freeze up at the register, or do they also happen at other times when you're not frozen?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the temporal relationship between the hallucinations (voices) and the disorganized behavior (freezing), which is not specifically addressed in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't really know if they happen at the exact same time. It's hard to tell. They definitely happen at other times, though, like when I'm just stocking shelves or wiping down the counter. 

Counters are so hard to keep clean, especially with the hand sanitizer dispenser right there. People always pump it too hard and it drips down the side of the cabinet and onto the floor. It leaves this sticky spot that catches all the dirt from people's shoes. I tried scrubbing it with this heavy-duty degreaser we have in the back, but the smell gave me a terrible headache. It smelled like cheap pine needles and chemicals. My grandmother used to use Pine-Sol on her kitchen floors. She had this old linoleum that was patterned to look like brick, but it was peeling in the corners. She used to make the best snickerdoodles in that kitchen. She'd let me roll the dough in the cinnamon sugar before she put them on the baking sheet. I still remember the way the kitchen smelled when they were baking. I tried to find her recipe after she passed away, but it was just written on the back of an old envelope and I think it got thrown out. 

But, um, yeah, I'm not really sure if the voices happen when I freeze up. They just happen kind of throughout the day, you know?

inference.note: Auditory hallucinations (third-person commentary/command-like, occurring independently of freezing episodes) support a primary psychotic disorder (F20.9) alongside catatonia-like freezing behavior. The circumstantial, tangential speech with excessive irrelevant detail is consistent with disorganized thought process seen in schizophrenia, but could also reflect a psychotic disorder due to another medical condition (F06.1) if an organic cause for both catatonic features and hallucinations is found. Absence of automatisms (lip-smacking, fumbling) and retained awareness during freezing episodes make temporal lobe seizures (G40.909) less likely, though still not fully excluded given brief episodic freezing.

doctor.intent: Assess for postictal signs (confusion, fatigue, tongue biting, incontinence) after freezing episodes to help distinguish a seizure disorder from a primary psychotic or catatonic process
doctor.question: After you 'snap out of' one of these freezing episodes, do you notice feeling unusually tired, confused, sore, or having bitten your tongue or lost control of your bladder—things that might suggest your body just went through a seizure?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about postictal symptoms (fatigue, confusion, soreness, tongue biting, incontinence) to rule out seizures as a cause of the freezing episodes. My symptom profile does not contain information about postictal states or seizure symptoms.

patient.answer:
No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm usually a little tired after a long shift, but not unusually tired or anything. And I definitely haven't bitten my tongue or peed my pants or anything like that. That sounds awful. 

I did bite my tongue really bad once when I was a kid, though. I was riding my bike down this huge hill near my house—we called it Dead Man's Hill. It was so steep that if you didn't hit the brakes right at the bottom, you'd go flying right into Mr. Henderson's prize-winning rose bushes. He was so protective of those roses. He used to sit on his porch with a glass of iced tea just watching them. It was sweet tea, the real Southern kind where you boil the water with the sugar already in it so it dissolves perfectly. My wife tried to make sweet tea like that once, but she used Splenda and it just wasn't the same. It had this weird metallic aftertaste. We ended up pouring the whole pitcher down the sink. The sink in our kitchen drains really slow anyway. I think there's a clog somewhere deep in the pipes. I tried using that liquid drain cleaner, the thick gel kind that's supposed to eat through hair and grease, but it didn't really do much. I probably need to call a plumber, but they charge an arm and a leg just to show up. 

But, uh, no. I don't feel confused or sore or anything like that after I freeze up. I just kind of go back to ringing up the groceries.

inference.note: Absence of postictal confusion, tongue biting, or incontinence after freezing episodes argues against a seizure disorder, ruling out G40.909. Persistent auditory hallucinations occurring independently of the freezing episodes, combined with tangential thought process, support a primary psychotic disorder (F20.9), while catatonia-like freezing episodes without another identified medical cause keep F06.1 as a differential.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical, neurological, or substance-related cause that could explain the catatonic freezing episodes, to differentiate a primary psychotic disorder from a catatonic disorder due to a general medical condition
doctor.question: Do you have any medical conditions—like thyroid problems, seizures, head injuries, or recent illnesses—or do you use alcohol or drugs, that started around the same time these freezing episodes and voices began?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical conditions (thyroid problems, seizures, head injuries, recent illnesses) or substance use (alcohol, drugs) that might be causing the symptoms. The symptom profile does not contain information about medical history or substance use.

patient.answer:
No, I don't have any medical problems like that. My thyroid is fine, I think, and I definitely haven't hit my head. And I don't do drugs. I might have a beer on the weekend or something, but that's it. 

My brother is the one who's really into beer. He actually brews his own in his garage. It smells awful when he's doing it, like boiling yeast and old bread. He's got all these giant glass jugs—carboys, he calls them—lined up on his workbench. That workbench is incredible, actually. He built it himself out of reclaimed barn wood. He drove all the way out to Pennsylvania with his trailer to get the wood from this guy who was tearing down a dairy barn from the 1800s. The wood is so heavy. It's oak, I think. Or maybe chestnut? They used to use a lot of chestnut before that blight wiped them all out in the early nineteen-hundreds. It's a real shame. I read an article once that said the entire East Coast used to be covered in American chestnut trees, and the canopy was so thick that a squirrel could travel from Maine to Georgia without ever touching the ground. Can you imagine that? Just jumping from branch to branch for hundreds of miles. 

But, um, what was the question? Oh, right, illnesses and stuff. No, I haven't been sick or started drinking heavy or anything like that when all this started. I'm pretty healthy.

inference.note: Ruled out F06.1 given absence of medical conditions, head injury, substance use, or postictal symptoms that would suggest a catatonia due to another medical condition; the persistent hallucinations, disorganized/tangential speech, and catatonic-like freezing episodes without medical etiology support primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia).

doctor.intent: Determine the total duration of symptoms to assess the 6-month criterion for schizophrenia
doctor.question: How long have you been experiencing these voices and freezing episodes in total—did they start a few weeks ago, or have they been going on for several months or longer?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and the more clearly out-of-place moments have been happening for about the last three months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the voices and freezing episodes, which corresponds directly to the 'Psychotic Symptoms Duration' item in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I'd say the voices and those times where I just kind of... stop, the freezing up, it's been about three months now. Three months. 

That was right around the time the leaves started changing. Autumn is my favorite time of year, honestly. The colors are just spectacular, especially up in the mountains. My wife and I used to rent this little cabin up near Asheville every October. It had this wraparound porch with a hot tub on the back deck. Sitting in that hot tub with a cup of coffee while the air was crisp and the leaves were falling... there's really nothing like it. We stopped going, though, after they raised the rental rates. It just got too expensive, you know? Everything is getting so expensive these days. I went to buy a carton of eggs the other day and I couldn't believe the price. It makes you want to start raising your own chickens. My neighbor, Gary, he has chickens in his backyard. He built this elaborate coop out of old pallets and chicken wire. He even put a little ramp in for them to walk up. Sometimes he brings us over a dozen fresh eggs. They taste so much better than the ones from the store. The yolks are this deep, rich orange color instead of pale yellow. You can really tell the difference when you make an omelet. 

But yeah, three months. That's about how long it's been going on.

inference.note: Confirmed symptom duration of ~3 months (hallucinations plus catatonic-like freezing), which exceeds the 1-month threshold required for schizophrenia and rules out brief psychotic disorder (F23). No evidence of seizure activity, substance use, or medical illness to suggest an organic cause, and no mood symptoms to suggest schizoaffective disorder. Findings remain consistent with schizophrenia, unspecified.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the total duration of psychotic and related symptoms (including any prodromal changes) has been less than or more than 6 months, to distinguish schizophrenia from schizophreniform or brief psychotic disorder
doctor.question: Before these voices and freezing episodes started three months ago, did you notice any earlier changes—like becoming more withdrawn, having trouble concentrating, or feeling like something was 'off'—that may have begun even further back, say four to six months ago or more?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building for about two years and four months, since my youngest left the Eastern Shore for college.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of earlier changes (prodromal symptoms) before the onset of the psychotic symptoms, which corresponds to the overall duration of the illness.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I guess things were feeling off long before the freezing up started. It's actually been building for a while... about two years and four months, I'd say. That was right since my youngest left the Eastern Shore for college. 

The Eastern Shore is really beautiful, you know. We used to go out there and get those big bushel baskets of blue crabs. You lay out the newspaper on the picnic table and just go at them with those little wooden mallets. The Old Bay seasoning gets absolutely everywhere. It gets under your fingernails, and if you have a papercut you didn't know about, boy, you feel it then. My youngest loved it out there. But then he packed up his Honda Civic to head off to school. It was one of those older Civics, the ones that run forever if you just remember to change the oil. I always told him, "Check the oil every time you get gas," but kids don't listen. They just rely on the dashboard lights. The check engine light came on once when we were driving to a hardware store. I was going to buy caulk for the bathtub because the grout was getting all dark and moldy. I saw this video online about how to scrape it out and redo it. It looked so easy in the video, but the guy had this special oscillating power tool. I just had a flathead screwdriver, and let me tell you, it took me all weekend to scrape that old stuff out. My knees were killing me by Sunday night from kneeling on the tile. 

But, um... yeah. Two years and four months. That's when I started feeling like things were changing, right after he left.

inference.note: Chronic course (~2 years 4 months) with prodromal decline after son left, followed by persistent auditory hallucinations (3 months) unrelated temporally to catatonia-like freezing episodes, no LOC/postictal signs, no substance/medical cause, tangential/circumstantial speech throughout - consistent with schizophrenia with catatonic features. No new alternative diagnoses introduced; candidate list unchanged.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the patient's visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
